column1: # Parity cases: persist. Same six tab-separated columns.
#   expr <TAB> a <TAB> b <TAB> c <TAB> expect <TAB> name
# Both runners build their fixtures in the SAME scratch directory,
# /tmp/parity_persist, which is deliberate: it makes the path inside an error
# message identical in both trees, so the message can be compared verbatim
# rather than through a filter. Setup writes good.json, broken.json and
# empty.json; absent.json is never written by anyone.
# THE STATUS WORDS ARE THE CASE FILE'S, NOT EITHER TREE'S. gBASIC's
# read_status answers loaded/missing/corrupt; Python's returns a tervalue
# Outcome and answers ok/unknown/invalid, which is a deliberate deviation
# documented in etools/persist.py. Both runners map into the vocabulary below,
# so what these cases test is the CLASSIFICATION -- that the same file lands
# in the same one of three buckets in both trees. The naming difference is
# covered by the unit tests and the module docstring, not here.
#   loaded   <-  status = "loaded"   |  Outcome.is_ok
#   missing  <-  status = "missing"  |  Outcome.is_unknown
#   corrupt  <-  status = "corrupt"  |  Outcome.is_invalid
# There is no `reports absent` case. gBASIC leaves message empty for a missing
# file; Python fills reason with "no file at <path>", because collapsing
# "not there" and "could not be read" into one unknown means the reason is the
# only thing that tells them apart. An intentional divergence, not a defect,
# so it is stated here rather than dressed up as a shared expectation.
